name: Lateral geniculate nucleus
summary: A small six-layered nucleus under the pulvinar where the optic tract ends. Fibers from the contralateral eye reach layers 1, 4 and 6 and those from the ipsilateral eye layers 2, 3 and 5, so each geniculate maps the contralateral visual hemifield; magnocellular layers 1–2 handle motion and contrast, parvocellular layers 3–6 detail and color. Its axons form the optic radiation to the calcarine cortex. Its dual blood supply from the anterior choroidal and lateral posterior choroidal arteries explains the sector-shaped field defects of geniculate infarcts.

anatomy.location: Ventrolateral to the pulvinar on the inferior surface of the posterior thalamus, lateral to the medial geniculate body and above the hippocampus, at the end of the optic tract; the brachium of the superior colliculus passes medial to it.

function: Thalamic relay of the visual pathway; gates and sharpens retinal signals under cortical and brainstem control before they reach the primary visual cortex.

bestView.label: lateral geniculate body at the end of the optic tract, medial to the temporal horn
LGN below the pulvinar and above the hippocampus

imaging.normalAppearance: A small bump on the inferolateral thalamus at the termination of the optic tract, visible on thin coronal T2 and as the MASSP mesh in this atlas; lesions are small and easily missed.

pathology.finding: Small restriction at the lateral geniculate body giving a congruous homonymous defect, often a horizontal sectoranopia (lateral posterior choroidal) or upper-and-lower quadrant loss with sparing of the horizontal sector (anterior choroidal).
Atrophy of the LGN years after an eye or optic tract lesion; imaging is subtle.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Lateral posterior choroidal artery infarct of the middle of the nucleus

lesionEffects.deficit: Upper and lower quadrantic loss sparing the horizontal sector
lesionEffects.mechanism: Anterior choroidal artery infarct of the medial and lateral parts
Pupillary fibers leave the optic tract before the geniculate

examination: Confrontation fields and formal perimetry: look for congruous sector defects
Pupillary light reflex (preserved, unlike optic tract lesions with RAPD)
pearls: A wedge-shaped homonymous defect pointing to fixation is a geniculate lesion
Geniculate and cortical lesions spare the pupils; optic tract lesions do not
